title: Next-Gen AI Unleashed: GPU-Free Models, Real-time Video Editing, and Robotic Intelligence Surge
summary: This week in AI saw groundbreaking developments, notably Muan's Longat 2.0, a 1.6 trillion-parameter model trained entirely on non-Nvidia ASICs, signaling a significant shift in AI hardware reliance. Anthropic re-released Claude Fable 5 globally, but with stringent usage limitations and performance reductions, sparking debate among users. Alongside these major releases, innovations in real-time video editing (Liveedit), advanced 3D hand reconstruction (Vidi Hand), and physically accurate 3D simulations (PhySyFormer) pushed creative boundaries. Robotics also saw significant strides with Agents A1 offering a powerful, consumer-runnable agentic model, while Omni Contact and Nvidia Aspire introduced sophisticated frameworks for humanoid robot learning and skill acquisition.
article:
The world of artificial intelligence continues its relentless pace of innovation, with a flurry of significant announcements this week spanning groundbreaking hardware independence, advanced model capabilities, and transformative applications in vision and robotics. From a Chinese food delivery giant training a frontier model without Nvidia GPUs to new systems for real-time video editing and sophisticated robotic learning, the landscape of AI is rapidly evolving.

One of the most impactful revelations comes from Chinese food delivery company Muan, which unveiled its latest open-source model, **Longat 2.0**. What makes this release particularly monumental is not just its impressive performance, but the fact that this 1.6 trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model was trained entirely without Nvidia GPUs. Instead, Muan leveraged specialized AI ASICs (Application-Specific Integrated Circuits), rumored to be Huawei chips, for its entire training and deployment. This achievement directly challenges Nvidia's dominance in AI hardware and underscores China's accelerating drive towards technological self-sufficiency. The stability of the training process, with "no rollbacks or irreversible loss spikes," further validates the maturity and reliability of these alternative hardware platforms for frontier-scale AI development. Longat 2.0 is designed for complex agentic coding and long-context tasks, demonstrating performance that rivals leading closed models like GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus, even surpassing Google's Gemini 3.1 Pro in certain agentic coding and reasoning benchmarks. Despite its colossal size (the FP8 version alone is over 2TB), its open-source release under the MIT license offers immense potential for the AI community, with expectations for quantized versions to emerge for broader accessibility.

In a highly anticipated move, Anthropic re-released **Claude Fable 5** globally after an earlier ban by the U.S. government. Positioned as one of the most powerful models available, Fable 5's return comes with notable caveats. Users can access it via a subscription plan until July 7th, after which it transitions to usage credits. Crucially, access is capped at 50% of weekly usage limits, a restriction that many users have found severely limiting. Furthermore, the re-released version appears to be "nerfed" compared to its initial iteration. Anthropic explicitly states that "some routine tasks like coding and debugging will fall back to Opus 4.8," a significant drawback given Fable 5's reported strengths in agentic coding workflows. This perceived castration is attributed to an "improved safety classifier" designed to block jailbreak attempts, which unfortunately leads to more false positives and the rejection of benign requests. Benchmarks suggest reduced hallucination but a notable performance drop in debugging and refactoring tasks, with mixed results across other metrics. This re-release highlights the tension between powerful AI capabilities and regulatory demands for safety, resulting in a model that is both highly capable yet heavily constrained and expensive.

Adding to Anthropic's recent releases, **Claude Sonnet 5** also made its debut, positioned as a smaller variant. However, this model has drawn criticism for its performance and cost-effectiveness. Benchmarks indicate that Sonnet 5 often underperforms its older counterpart, Opus 4.8, and lags significantly behind competitors like GPT-5.5 and even the open-source GLM 5.2 in terms of intelligence and speed. Compounding these performance issues is its pricing, which is reportedly more than double that of GPT-5.5, despite being less capable. This makes Sonnet 5 an arguably less attractive option compared to existing, more performant, and cost-efficient models.

Beyond the realm of large language models, several other innovations showcased the breadth of AI research. **Musev VIT** introduces an AI model specifically designed for reading and understanding sheet music. Unlike general vision models, Musev VIT comprehends the complex interplay of symbols, timing, pitch, staff lines, spacing, and structure within musical notation. Trained on an extensive dataset of 9.7 million pages of sheet music, the model learns to reconstruct masked sections, thereby internalizing the intricate logic of musical scores. Its compact size (under 500 MB) makes it suitable for deployment on most consumer devices, filling a crucial gap in multimodal AI understanding.

For visual content creation, **Liveedit** offers real-time video editing capabilities, processing changes at nearly 13 frames per second. Users can simply provide a reference video and a text prompt to perform versatile edits, from changing clothing and weather to object removal and style transformations. This is achieved by adapting a traditional video model into a "causal chunk-wise streaming setup," allowing for continuous processing without requiring the entire video upfront. The system, along with its training script, is open-source and relatively compact at 17 GB, making it accessible for mid-to-high-end GPUs.

In the domain of 3D reconstruction, **Vidi Hand** stands out by accurately reconstructing 3D hand movements from video. This is a particularly challenging task due to the speed of hand movements, frequent occlusion, and the high sensitivity to small errors. Vidi Hand surpasses existing models in precision, capturing exact finger positions even when parts of the hand are obscured. This technology holds significant implications for training humanoid robots, where accurate hand manipulation data is critical, as well as for advancing augmented and virtual reality applications. The code for Vidi Hand is slated for an upcoming release.

Further enhancing robotic intelligence, **Agents A1** emerges as a medium-sized (35 billion parameters) Mixture-of-Experts model tailored for agentic workflows. Remarkably, despite its relatively smaller scale, Agents A1 demonstrates superior performance on various benchmarks, even outcompeting trillion-parameter models like Kimik K 2.6 and Deepseek V4 Pro, and in some scientific and instruction-following tasks, it even surpasses GPT-5.5. Its open-source nature and efficient design, with quantized versions as small as 21 GB, make it a strong contender for the new leading consumer-grade model runnable on offline hardware.

In advanced humanoid robotics, **Omni Contact** provides a framework for teaching robots long, complex, multi-step tasks that combine movement and interaction with objects. By introducing "contact flow," a compact plan for how a robot's body should move and make contact over time, Omni Contact enables robots to fluidly chain skills, recover from errors, and perform multi-step tasks for extended periods. Its high success rates in tasks like carrying boxes and pushing suitcases, coupled with its ability to integrate with vision models for semantic tasks, pushes humanoid robots closer to handling real-world complexity. The code and dataset for Omni Contact are open-sourced, fostering further research.

Finally, **PhySyFormer** addresses a critical gap in 3D content generation by predicting how 3D objects move and bend realistically under physical forces. Unlike many AI 3D generators that produce rigid models, PhySyFormer takes an object's shape, initial position, speed, and material type (e.g., rigid metal or elastic rubber) to generate physically accurate animations. Trained on over 100,000 simulated trajectories, it outperforms older methods in adhering to real physics laws, even for novel shapes and multiple interacting objects. With its code released and dataset forthcoming, PhySyFormer promises to bring unprecedented realism to 3D simulations.

And in another development for robotics, **Nvidia's Aspire** system focuses on self-improving robot learning. Aspire enables robots to learn from their own failed attempts, automatically converting these lessons into reusable skills. By writing robot control programs as code, executing them, observing outcomes, and then autonomously repairing and validating the code if errors occur, Aspire transforms failure into valuable knowledge. This innovative approach promises to drastically reduce the repetitive and often inefficient nature of traditional robot training, allowing robots to build a robust library of adaptable skills.

These diverse advancements underscore the rapid and multifaceted progress in AI, from overcoming hardware dependencies and refining large language models to enabling more intelligent and physically aware robotic systems. The coming months are set to witness even more profound shifts as these technologies mature and integrate into real-world applications.
